newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S., Japan to send emissaries to China.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan to send emissaries to China.

text.p: Japan and the United States decided on Sunday to swiftly send emissaries to China and other Asian nations to explain new security arrangements that would give Tokyo its highest military profile since World War two.

Japan's enhanced military role in the Asia-Pacific region, announced by U.S. and Japanese officials in Honolulu on Saturday, set off tremors both in Japan itself and Asian nations that suffered under Tokyo's World War two occupation.

Japanese worried the new role might breach their pacifist constitution, China was concerned it was aimed at containing its growing economic and military power and some Asian nations saw the new ties as a sign of rising Japanese militarism.
The new arrangements were revealed in an interim report on six months of negotiations to review the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, the basis of Washington's defence policy in Asia.
They include use of Japanese airfields by U.S. warplanes in a conflict, Japanese involvement in minesweeping, enhanced intelligence gathering by Tokyo and Japan peacekeeping duties.

The document says instability and uncertainty in Asia, despite the end of the Cold War, mean that Japan and the United States need an effective means to counter an armed attack on Japan or an armed conflict near Japan.

Japan's Kyodo News Service said the guidelines "appear to allow the U.S. to get Japan's assistance when the former dispatches troops in an emergency on the Korean Peninsula, the Taiwan Straits, the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea or anywhere else in areas surrounding Japan."

"This is the first time Japan is looking to do more than in the past," Navy Lieutennant Commander Karen Jeffries told reporters after Saturday's meeting in Hawaii of Japanese and U.S. defence and foreign affairs officials.
Despite the planned expansion, Tokyo has held out against direct combat in an armed conflict in Asia or elsewhere.
Japanese officials are wary of too broad a role because of a pacifist constitution, which bans offensive military actions.
A final report in November will spell out exact details of the new military cooperation, such as the number of air bases to be opened to U.S. warplanes in a future conflict.

"What this allows us to do is to focus on the situation in a post-Cold War world where there is no Soviet Union," said Frank Kramer, Assistant Secretary of Defence for International Security Affairs, who led the U.S. delegation in Honolulu.
Asked about concern voiced by China, Kramer said there was "nothing in the guidelines that should be of concern."
Tokyo and Washington worry that China may regard itself as the main target of the new arrangements, a view that Beijing expressed on the weekend.
In a report from Beijing, Kyodo said a top Chinese military officer told a delegation from Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party that China strongly opposed the new military ties.
China's Deputy Chief of General Staff of the People's Liberation Army, Xiong Guangkai, said the new guidelines represented continued Cold War-era thinking.
In a bid to allay Chinese concerns, top officials from Japan's Foreign Ministry and Defense Agency arrive in Beijing on Monday to explain the views of Washington and Tokyo.
The United States plans a similiar diplomatic offensive to Asian nations, including a visit by a so-far unnamed top Washington official to Beijing.

U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Charles Kartman plans a visit to South Korea while Curt Campbell, deputy assistant Secretary of Defense for East Asian and Pacific Affairs, will visit South East Asian nations.
"We should get neighbouring countries to rid themselves of their sense of uncertainty over what Japan would do in a crisis," a senior Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.

The furore in Japan about the new arrangements focussed on whether they violated the country's post-World War two pacifist constitution which confines its self-defence forces or military to protecting only Japanese territory.

In a bid to keep his options open in case there was too big a domestic backlash, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, a strong supporter of the new arrangements, said some areas of the new military ties were still unclear.
"Since it's an interim report, I suppose opinions differ (between Japan and the United States)," he told reporters.
Opposition leader Ichiro Ozawa, head of the conservative New Frontier Party, also a supporter of stronger U.S.-Japan military ties, said the debate should focus on Japan's constitution.
"Japan will be a lawless area if it takes measures beyond the law without discussing basic matters," he said.
